Variables: names for values

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
section: Bending stress — our first engineering formula
text:
Bending stress — our first engineering formula
For a rectangular cantilever (width b, thickness t, length L, load F):
\[\sigma = \frac{6 F L}{b\,t^2}\]

F = 1500      # N
L = 150       # mm
b = 40        # mm
t = 12        # mm
sigma_MPa = 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2)     # N/mm² = MPa
print(f"sigma = {sigma_MPa:.1f} MPa")

sigma = 234.4 MPa

for: repeat for every item

for t in [8, 10, 12, 16, 20]:
    sigma = 6 * 1500 * 150 / (40 * t ** 2)
    print(f"t = {t:2d} mm  ->  sigma = {sigma:6.1f} MPa")

t =  8 mm  ->  sigma =  527.3 MPa
t = 10 mm  ->  sigma =  337.5 MPa
t = 12 mm  ->  sigma =  234.4 MPa
t = 16 mm  ->  sigma =  131.8 MPa
t = 20 mm  ->  sigma =   84.4 MPa



t takes each value in turn; the indented block runs once per value
[8, 10, ...] is a list — more about lists in Session 2

range(): sequences of numbers

print(list(range(5)))          # 0 .. 4
print(list(range(2, 10, 2)))   # start, stop (excluded), step

[0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
[2, 4, 6, 8]

for load in range(500, 3001, 500):     # 500, 1000, ..., 3000 N
    total = total + load
print("sum of loads:", total)

sum of loads: 10500



the accumulator pattern: start with 0, add in each step

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
section: while: repeat until a condition changes
text:
while: repeat until a condition changes
Find the smallest thickness (step 0.5 mm) that gives SF ≥ 1.5:

t = 6.0
sf = 0
while sf < 1.5:
    t = t + 0.5
    sigma = 6 * 1500 * 150 / (40 * t ** 2)
    sf = 355 / sigma
print(f"minimum thickness: {t} mm (SF = {sf:.2f})")

minimum thickness: 12.0 mm (SF = 1.51)



Use for when you know what to loop over, while when you only know when to stop. Make sure the condition can become false, or the loop never ends (in Colab: ■ stop button).

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
break and continue

for t in [8, 10, 12, 14, 16]:
    sigma = 6 * 1500 * 150 / (40 * t ** 2)
    if sigma > 355:
        continue            # skip this one, go to the next t
    print(f"first acceptable thickness: {t} mm")
    break                   # leave the loop

first acceptable thickness: 10 mm

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
Why functions?
We already typed 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2) five times.

a function = a named, reusable piece of calculation
fewer copy-paste errors: fix the formula in one place
the name documents the intent: bending_stress(...)

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
Defining a function

def bending_stress(F, L, b, t):
    """Max bending stress of a rectangular cantilever, MPa (F in N, lengths in mm)."""
    return 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2)

s = bending_stress(1500, 150, 40, 12)
print(f"{s:.1f} MPa")

234.4 MPa



def name(parameters): + indented body
return sends the result back; without it, the function returns None
the text in """...""" is a docstring: what the function does, units

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
Default values and keyword arguments

def bending_stress(F, t, L=150, b=40):
    return 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2)

print(bending_stress(1500, 12))              # uses L=150, b=40
print(bending_stress(1500, 12, L=200))       # override one value
print(bending_stress(t=12, F=1500, b=50))    # keywords: any order

234.375
312.5
187.5



parameters with defaults go after the ones without
keyword arguments make calls readable: you see what each number means

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
Functions calling functions

def safety_factor(stress_MPa, yield_MPa=355):
    return yield_MPa / stress_MPa

def check_design(F, t):
    sf = safety_factor(bending_stress(F, t))
    status = "OK" if sf >= 1.5 else "FAIL"
    return f"F={F} N, t={t} mm: SF={sf:.2f} {status}"

print(check_design(1500, 12))
print(check_design(2500, 10))

F=1500 N, t=12 mm: SF=1.51 OK
F=2500 N, t=10 mm: SF=0.63 FAIL



"OK" if condition else "FAIL" — a one-line if

title: Python basics, control flow and functions
text:
Returning several values

def bracket_response(F, t, L=150, b=40, E=200_000):
    stress = 6 * F * L / (b * t ** 2)
    deflection = 4 * F * L ** 3 / (E * b * t ** 3)
    return stress, deflection

s, d = bracket_response(1500, 12)
print(f"stress {s:.1f} MPa, deflection {d:.3f} mm")

stress 234.4 MPa, deflection 1.465 mm



200_000 — underscores make long numbers readable
return a, b returns both; s, d = ... unpacks them

def area(b, t):

print(area(40, 12))

names created inside a function are local
pass data in through parameters, get it out with return

Acceptance criteria
A case passes only if all four hold:

accuracy is assessed on an independent test set, not the one used for tuning
error is in engineering terms — MaxAE as % of yield strength (or allowable deflection), not only R²
model behaviour outside the domain of applicability is shown

A formal R² = 0.99 without these points is not an acceptance.

title: Your environment and version control
text:
What is actually installed?

Python interpreter — the program that runs your code (python)
packages — extra libraries: NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn, …
pip — installs packages: pip install pandas
virtual environment — a separate folder with its own Python + packages for one project


Why separate environments? Project A needs pandas 2.1, project B needs 2.2. Without environments one of them breaks. With them, each project has exactly what it was tested with — the same idea as recording the solver version in a calculation report.

.gitignore: what Git should not track
.venv/
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
*.log

environments, temporary files, large generated results
never commit passwords or confidential data


Calculation results from a confidential project do not belong in a public repository. Keep code public or private on GitHub, data where your organisation allows.

title: Your environment and version control
text:
Undoing things
git restore bracket.py            # throw away uncommitted changes in a file
git restore --staged bracket.py   # un-add (keep the changes)
git checkout a41f2c9 -- bracket.py  # get the file as it was in that commit

Everything committed can be recovered. Uncommitted work cannot — commit often.

git pull                          # get changes made elsewhere

title: Visualisation
text:
Colour maps: choose on purpose

sequential (one quantity, low → high): viridis, Blues, Greys
diverging (around a meaningful centre, e.g. error = 0): PuOr, RdGy
qualitative (categories): the default colour cycle, tab10
avoid jet / rainbow: invents boundaries, unreadable in greyscale and for colour-blind readers


Reports get printed in black and white. Check: does the plot still work in greyscale? Use line styles and markers, not only colour.

text:
One cleaning function

def clean_bracket(path):
    """Read and clean a raw bracket export. Returns (clean DataFrame, report dict)."""
    df = pd.read_csv(path, sep=";", decimal=",")
    report = {"rows_in": len(df)}
    for c in ["load_N", "max_stress_MPa"]:
        df[c] = to_number(df[c])
    df = df.drop_duplicates()
    df.loc[df["load_N"] < 10, "load_N"] *= 1000                      # kN -> N
    df["E_GPa"] = df["E_GPa"].fillna(200.0)
    df = df[df["solver_status"] == "converged"]
    df = df[df["thickness_mm"].between(8, 20)]
    df = df.dropna(subset=["max_stress_MPa", "deflection_mm"])
    df["safety_factor"] = 355 / df["max_stress_MPa"]                  # recompute, consistent
    report["rows_out"] = len(df)
    return df.reset_index(drop=True), report

data, rep = clean_bracket("data/bracket_raw.csv")

def validate(df):
    assert df["run_id"].is_unique, "duplicate run IDs"
    assert df.notna().all().all(), "missing values left"
    assert df["thickness_mm"].between(8, 20).all(), "thickness out of plan range"
    assert df["load_N"].between(200, 3000).all(), "load out of plan range (unit?)"
    assert (df["max_stress_MPa"] > 0).all(), "non-positive stress"
    return True

title: Data fundamentals
section: How do we choose the inputs?
text:
How do we choose the inputs?
Each calculation costs time. Which points of the design space should we compute?

full factorial grid — every combination of a few levels per input
random sampling — uniform random values in each range
Latin hypercube (LHS) — random, but each input’s range is evenly covered

title: Data fundamentals
text:
Full factorial grid

from itertools import product

thickness = [8, 12, 16, 20]
radius = [1, 4, 8]
load = [500, 1500, 3000]

grid = list(product(thickness, radius, load))
print(len(grid), "runs")
print(grid[:4])

36 runs
[(8, 1, 500), (8, 1, 1500), (8, 1, 3000), (8, 4, 500)]



4 inputs × 10 levels = 10 000 runs. Grids grow exponentially with the number of inputs (“curse of dimensionality”). Fine for 2–3 inputs, too expensive beyond that.

title: Data fundamentals
text:
Random and Latin hypercube sampling









LHS: every one of the 16 columns and 16 rows contains exactly one point — good coverage with few runs.

title: Data fundamentals
section: Practical rules for a calculation plan
text:
Practical rules for a calculation plan

define the domain of applicability first: min and max of every input
include the corners and the centre (extremes are where models fail)
record everything: inputs, solver version, mesh, status, date
keep some runs aside for testing (Module 3)
automate: the plan is a table; the solver reads it and writes results in a table

title: NumPy: calculations on whole arrays
text:
Why NumPy?

import numpy as np
import time

t = list(range(1, 1_000_001))
start = time.perf_counter()
s_list = [6 * 1500 * 150 / (40 * x ** 2) for x in t]
t_list = time.perf_counter() - start

t_arr = np.arange(1, 1_000_001)
start = time.perf_counter()
s_arr = 6 * 1500 * 150 / (40 * t_arr ** 2.0)
t_np = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"list: {t_list*1000:.0f} ms   numpy: {t_np*1000:.0f} ms   ({t_list/t_np:.0f}× faster)")

list: 44 ms   numpy: 5 ms   (10× faster)



one operation on the whole array, executed in compiled code
the basis of pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch

section: Monte Carlo: scatter in the inputs
text:
Monte Carlo: scatter in the inputs
Thickness tolerance ±0.3 mm (= 3σ), load scatter 10 % (1σ):

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
N = 100_000
t = rng.normal(12, 0.1, N)
F = rng.normal(1500, 150, N)
sf = 355 / bending_stress(F, t)
print(f"mean SF {sf.mean():.2f}, 1st percentile {np.percentile(sf, 1):.2f}")
print(f"P(SF < 1.5) = {(sf < 1.5).mean():.2%}")

mean SF 1.53, 1st percentile 1.22
P(SF < 1.5) = 46.32%



100 000 evaluations in milliseconds — because the formula is cheap. With an FEM solver each point costs minutes. That is exactly why we want surrogate models.
